why: Marginal (unconditional) PD is the raw change in cumulative PD; conditional PD divides that by the survival probability to t-1.
Same year-t unconditional PD: from cumulative PD it is later minus earlier, Cum(t)-Cum(t-1); from survival it is earlier minus later, PS(t-1)-PS(t).
1-e^{-lambda t} is the cumulative default probability; e^{-lambda t} by itself is the survival probability.
The average hazard rate is spread/(1-RR). A forward hazard between years 3 and 5 needs time-weighting of the averages, (5*lambda5 - 3*lambda3)/2, not a plain difference.
d1 uses (r + sigma^2/2); distance to default is d2 and uses (r - sigma^2/2), i.e. d1 minus sigma*sqrt(T).
N(d1) is the equity delta that links equity volatility to asset volatility; N(-d2) is the risk-neutral PD. Don't swap d1 and d2.
Risk-neutral PD N(-d2) drifts at the risk-free rate r; real-world PD drifts at the expected asset return mu, so it is lower when mu > r.
Equity is a long call on firm assets, max(V-F,0); debt is face value minus a put, F - max(F-V,0).
EL is linear, EA*PD*LR. UL is EA*sqrt(PD*var_LR + LR^2*var_PD): variances go in, and LR is squared only on the PD-variance term.
Portfolio EL is a simple sum of individual ELs; portfolio UL is not additive and needs the correlation-weighted double sum under a square root.
sqrt(n + rho(n^2-n)) scales UL_i up to total portfolio UL; the per-loan contribution divides that by n, giving sqrt(1/n + rho(1-1/n)).
Same algebra, sqrt(n + n(n-1)rho)/n. In CR-4 it multiplies a loan's UL to get its UL contribution; in CR-19 it is the netting factor on exposure.
The exact n-loan contribution keeps the 1/n terms; the large-portfolio shortcut drops them, leaving UL_i*sqrt(rho).
Portfolio economic capital multiplies UL_P by CM; a single deal's capital multiplies its UL contribution (ULC_i) by CM, not its standalone UL_i.
Both are Euler risk contributions that sum to the total. The UL contribution uses the correlation-weighted UL over UL_P; component VaR uses beta_i*w_i*VaR_p.
Margin received is the value above the threshold plus initial margin. The credit support amount also nets out what you would post (-value above K_p) and subtracts collateral C already held.
Expected loss uses the expected PD; the unexpected loan loss for RAROC replaces PD with alpha, an extreme (unexpected) default rate.

Both RAROCs net expected losses and tax out of the numerator. The difference is the denominator: credit RAROC divides loan revenues, loan value x (s + f - l - c)(1 - x), by capital at risk (the duration-based change in loan value, -L x D x di/(1+i)). Operational-risk RAROC divides after-tax risk-adjusted net income by economic capital.
There are two RAROC denominators: a market-based one from duration, -L*D*delta_i/(1+i), and an experience-based one, alpha*LGD*EAD.
CVA weights the counterparty's default probabilities q_i by our loss v_i; DVA weights our own default probabilities q*_i by the counterparty's loss v*_i.
Sign convention: Hull subtracts a positive CVA and adds DVA (f_nd - CVA + DVA). Gregory writes BCVA = CVA + DVA, with CVA carrying a negative sign.
CVA uses EPE with the counterparty's LGD and PD; DVA uses ENE with the institution's own LGD and PD.
The CVA term uses EPE with counterparty LGD_C and PD_C; the DVA term uses ENE with own LGD_I and PD_I.
The conditional PD has -sqrt(rho)*F. WCDR has +sqrt(rho)*N^{-1}(X) because the worst-case factor is F = -N^{-1}(X).
Hull's Credit VaR, L(1-R)*WCDR, is the worst-case loss with no EL deducted; CR-11's credit VaR subtracts EL from the percentile loss.
The CR-10 capital requirement is the worst-case loss sum(WCDR*EAD*LGD); Basel IRB capital subtracts expected loss, i.e. worst-case minus EL.
beta_i*beta_j is the asset-return correlation; default correlation is much smaller and needs the bivariate normal, (Phi2(k,k;beta^2) - pi^2)/(pi(1-pi)).
These are the same identity solved in opposite directions: CR-11 gives default correlation from the joint PD; MR-8 gives the joint PD as rho*sqrt(...) + PD_A*PD_B.
'Firm 1 alone' subtracts the joint probability, pi1 - pi12; 'neither' must add pi12 back, 1 - pi1 - pi2 + pi12.
AR from the CAP curve is the area ratio A_R/A_P; AR from the ROC curve is 2*AUROC - 1. Don't report AUROC itself as AR.
DTI is debt payments over income (lower is safer); DSCR is net operating income over debt service (higher is safer). They are near-inverses.
LTV measures collateral coverage (mortgage over appraised value); DTI measures affordability (monthly debt payments over gross monthly income).
To go from SMM to CPR, raise (1-SMM) to the power 12; to go from CPR to SMM, use the power 1/12. Don't just multiply or divide by 12.
100 PSA ramps CPR by 0.2% a month and caps at 6% from month 30; the PSA multiple divides the actual CPR by that benchmark and multiplies by 100.
The delinquency ratio counts receivables more than 90 days overdue; the default ratio counts receivables already written off.
MPR is card principal plus interest collected over total receivables; SMM is only prepayments (beyond scheduled principal) over the outstanding pool balance.
EE uses the fixed multiplier 0.4 (the mean of the positive part of a normal); PFE uses the confidence-level quantile k, e.g. 1.65 or 2.33.
The premium leg is weighted by survival probability times spread; the protection leg is weighted by PD times (1 - recovery).
MtM to the protection seller is PV(payments) - PV(payoff), and the buyer's is the reverse. With a fixed coupon, price = 100 - 100*D*(s - c), so s > c means the buyer pays upfront.

The first is the constant-EPE shortcut: CVA divided by the CDS premium term equals minus the counterparty's CDS spread times average EPE; the second divides an already computed CVA by risky duration times notional.
Loan stressed EL stresses only PD, with EAD fixed; derivative stressed EL stresses both PD and EPE, and EAD = EPE*alpha.
Stress loss on CVA ignores own default. Stress loss on BCVA includes stressed DVA, which partly offsets it because own spreads also widen.
Arithmetic return subtracts 1 from the price ratio; the log return takes ln of the same ratio (log returns add up over time, arithmetic ones don't).
P/L VaR is already in dollars; VaR from return data uses return mu and sigma and must be multiplied by P_{t-1}.
Normal VaR is linear, (-mu + sigma z) x P; lognormal VaR is P x (1 - e^{mu - sigma z}), so it can never exceed the position value.
99% VaR uses 2.326 sigma and 97.5% ES uses 2.338 sigma. They are almost equal, which is why FRTB treats them as roughly equivalent; don't swap the confidence levels.
Normal ES is mu + sigma x phi(z)/(1 - confidence), so tail density over tail probability rather than z; at 97.5% this gives the 2.338 multiplier.
A quantile's standard error divides sqrt(p(1-p)/n) by the density f(q); the exception z-test's denominator is sqrt(p(1-p)T), the SD of a count, which multiplies by T.
The confidence interval is q ± se(q) x z; se(q) itself is sqrt(p(1-p)/n)/f(q). Don't leave out the density or the z multiplier.
The expected number of exceedances is np (alpha x n), but the historical-simulation VaR is the next observation, (alpha x n) + 1.
Failure rate N/T is a proportion to compare with p; the expected exception count pT (np) is a number to compare with N.
The z-test is the normal approximation (x - pT)/sqrt(p(1-p)T); the binomial formula gives the exact probability of exactly x exceptions.
LR_uc tests frequency only (chi-square with 1 df, critical value 3.84); LR_cc = LR_uc + LR_ind also tests independence (2 df, critical value 5.99).
Unconditional coverage (1 df) versus conditional coverage, which adds LR_ind for clustering (2 df).
KS takes the single maximum absolute gap |z_j - A_j|; Cramer-von Mises sums the squared gaps from (2j-1)/2n over all points and adds 1/(12n).
Anderson-Darling uses log terms that put extra weight on the tails; Cramer-von Mises weights every squared deviation equally.
GEV with xi not zero uses (1 + xi(x - mu)/sigma)^(-1/xi) inside exp[-.] (Frechet if xi > 0); with xi = 0 it becomes the double exponential (Gumbel).
GPD with xi not zero is 1 - [1 + xi x/beta]^(-1/xi); with xi = 0 it reduces to the exponential 1 - exp(-x/beta).
GEV (block maxima) is exp[-(1 + xi z)^(-1/xi)] with location mu; GPD (peaks over threshold) is 1 - (1 + xi x/beta)^(-1/xi) on excesses over u, with no mu.
F_u(x) is the conditional distribution of excesses over u, [F(x+u) - F(u)]/[1 - F(u)]; the GPD is the parametric limit that approximates it.
Principal mapping uses the VaR at the portfolio's average maturity; duration mapping uses the VaR interpolated at the portfolio's duration, which is lower.
Undiversified cash-flow VaR simply adds PV x VaR% (correlation = 1); the ordering principal > duration > diversified refers to the diversified cash-flow VaR.

MR-6 estimates marginal VaR directly as the slope of a regression of the position's value change on the portfolio's value change; IM-5 computes it analytically as (VaR_p / portfolio value) x beta_i, with beta_i = cov(R_i,R_p)/sigma_p^2.
Inverse relationships: correlation = cov/(sigma_i sigma_j), and a covariance-matrix entry = rho x sigma_i x sigma_j.
Same portfolio variance: the explicit two-asset form needs 2 w_X w_Y cov; the matrix form sqrt(beta_h C beta_v) takes position weights around the covariance matrix.
The Pearson joint PD is rho x sqrt(PD_A(1 - PD_A) PD_B(1 - PD_B)) + PD_A PD_B; the single-factor model uses a bivariate normal Phi_2(k, k; beta^2) instead.
The full process adds the shock sigma epsilon sqrt(dt) and scales drift by dt; the deterministic form gives only the expected change a(mu - S_{t-1}).
F02 gives the change S_t - S_{t-1}; F03 gives the level, so add S_{t-1} back.
The mean reversion rate a = (S_t - S_{t-1})/(mu - S_{t-1}); autocorrelation is 1 - a, so strong mean reversion means low autocorrelation.

The regression form writes the one-step change as a mu - a S_{t-1} (intercept a mu, slope -a on S_{t-1}); the other solves directly for the reversion rate a as the observed change divided by the gap mu - S_{t-1}.
Autocorrelation correlates a series (correlations) with its own one-period lag; the ordinary correlation coefficient relates two different series.
Same mean-reverting drift shape: in correlations it is a(mu - S) per period; in Vasicek it is k(theta - r)dt plus a sigma dw shock.
One discrete step closes a fraction a of the gap; Vasicek's continuous expectation decays the gap by e^{-kT} over T years.
The DV01-neutral hedge uses the DV01 ratio only; the regression hedge multiplies that same ratio by beta.
The regression hedge scales the DV01-ratio face amount by the yield beta; a reverse regression swaps the axes, so its implied risk weight is the reciprocal of its own slope, 1/beta, not beta itself.
F05 defines beta^10 as the negative DV01-weighted ratio; F07 solves for the face amount F^10 = -(F^20 DV01^20/DV01^10) x beta^10. Watch the sign and which DV01 is in the denominator.
Same structure: F^10 uses DV01^10 and beta^10, while F^30 uses DV01^30 and beta^30. Don't mix up the hedge instrument's DV01.
Change-on-change regresses Delta y on Delta x; level-on-level regresses y on x, and its errors are often persistent (AR(1)).

The level regression explains y_t as alpha + beta x_t plus an error; the AR(1) equation models that error itself, epsilon_t = rho epsilon_{t-1} + v_t, where rho is error autocorrelation, not the hedge beta.
The up-state condition uses the up-state discount factor (0.987654) and payoff 0; the down-state condition uses 0.992556 and payoff 2.556.
The zero price discounts at one spot rate squared, (1 + r(2))^2; the chained version uses the product of the two one-year rates (1 + r1)(1 + r2).

The pure-expectations 2-year spot rate chains today's one-year rate r_1 with the expected one-year rate next year r_2: sqrt((1+r_1)(1+r_2)) - 1; Jensen's inequality E[1/(1+r)] > 1/E(1+r) is the convexity effect that pushes actual yields below that.
The decomposition includes -D dr and the convexity term (1/2)C sigma^2 dt; the expected return for a risk-averse investor is r0 dt + lambda D dt, a duration-based risk premium.
Model 1 has no drift (dr = sigma dw); Model 2 adds a constant drift lambda dt.
Model 2 uses one constant lambda; Ho-Lee's lambda_t varies over time so the model can fit the term structure.
Ho-Lee's drift is an exogenous time-dependent lambda_t; Vasicek's drift k(theta - r) depends on the current rate (mean reversion).
Model 1's outer date-2 nodes are r0 ± 2 sigma sqrt(dt); Model 2 adds a drift of 2 lambda dt.
Model 2's date-2 drift is 2 lambda dt; Ho-Lee's is (lambda1 + lambda2)dt.
The tree moves ± sigma sqrt(dt) from r0; the SD of the rate change per step is sigma sqrt(dt), not sigma.
Equivalent forms: theta minus the decayed gap (theta - r0)e^{-kT}, or a weighted average r0 e^{-kT} + theta(1 - e^{-kT}). Don't put e^{-kT} on theta.
Vasicek half-life ln(2)/k is a time for the gap to halve; the Model 3 asymptote sigma/sqrt(2 alpha) is a cap on the terminal SD of the rate.
Ho-Lee is normal (dr has a time-dependent drift); Salomon Brothers is its lognormal counterpart, modeling d[ln r].
Vasicek's volatility is constant sigma (rates can go negative); CIR scales the volatility by sqrt(r).
Vasicek mean-reverts r in levels with constant parameters; Black-Karasinski mean-reverts ln r with time-dependent k(t), theta(t), sigma(t).
Model 3 gets a declining term structure of volatility from sigma e^{-alpha t} with time-dependent drift; Vasicek gets it from mean-reversion k(theta - r) with constant sigma.
The general model allows any sigma(t); Model 3 specifies an exponential decay sigma e^{-alpha t}.
Model 4 is dr = a r dt + sigma r dw, with drift and volatility proportional to r; Salomon Brothers models d ln r with a time-dependent drift a(t).
The lognormal Salomon tree multiplies: r0 e^{a1 dt + sigma sqrt(dt)}. The normal Ho-Lee tree adds: r0 + lambda1 dt + sigma sqrt(dt).
The up and down nodes differ only in the sign of sigma sqrt(dt) in the exponent; the drift a1 dt appears in both.
The up-up node has +2 sigma sqrt(dt) in the exponent; the middle ud node has no sigma term, only (a1 + a2)dt.
The Gauss+ short factor r reverts to m with no shock; the medium factor m reverts to l and has correlated shocks rho dW1 + sqrt(1 - rho^2) dW2.
The long factor l reverts to the constant mu and is driven only by dW1; the medium factor reverts to l and loads on both shocks.
Basic parity is c - p = S - PV(X); with a dividend yield, S becomes S0 e^{-qT} and the strike is discounted continuously as K e^{-rT}.
Because parity holds for both market and BSM prices, the market-minus-BSM error is the same for a put and a call with the same strike and maturity.
Measure 1 (bias) is the mean of D over the SD of A; Measure 2 (noise) is the variance of D over the variance of A.
The general copula maps marginals through any F^{-1} into joint F_n; the Gaussian copula uses the standard normal inverse N^{-1} and the multivariate normal M_n.
The default-time copula plugs cumulative default probabilities Q_i(t) into the Gaussian copula in place of generic marginals G_i(u_i).
Individual VaR uses the asset's own sigma_i times its position |w_i|P; diversified portfolio VaR uses sigma_p times the whole portfolio value P.
rho=1 means individual VaRs add linearly (undiversified); rho=0 means they combine as the square root of the sum of squares.
Diversified VaR uses sigma_p, which includes correlations below 1; undiversified VaR is just the sum of individual VaRs (rho=1), so it is always greater than or equal to diversified VaR.
Same marginal VaR: Z_c*cov(R_i,R_p)/sigma_p per dollar, equal to (VaR_p / portfolio value) x beta_i. Don't forget to divide VaR_p by the portfolio value.
Full revaluation computes VaR(P+A) - VaR(P) exactly; the shortcut is a linear approximation, MVaR_A times the dollar amount added.
Incremental VaR multiplies MVaR by the new position being added (the change); component VaR multiplies MVaR by the existing holding w_iP, and component VaRs sum to VaR_p.
Component VaR = VaR_p x beta_i x w_i (portfolio VaR scaled by beta) = VaR_i x rho_i (individual VaR scaled by correlation). Don't mix beta with rho.
Finite-N volatility is sigma*sqrt(1/N + (1-1/N)rho); as N goes to infinity the 1/N terms vanish and the floor is sigma*sqrt(rho).
The global minimum-risk portfolio equalises marginal VaR across assets; the optimal (max risk-adjusted return) portfolio equalises excess return divided by MVaR.
The VaR-based Sharpe ratio puts VaR_p in the denominator; the classic Sharpe ratio uses total return standard deviation sigma.
One-period VaR = Z x sigma_p(%) x P; the multi-day version starts from a dollar sigma_P and scales by sqrt(t), so don't multiply by P again.
IR divides alpha relative to a benchmark by tracking error (active risk); SR divides excess over the risk-free rate by total volatility sigma.
IR = alpha / tracking error is the definition (risk-adjusted alpha); Grinold's fundamental law gives the MAXIMUM attainable IR from skill and breadth, IC x sqrt(BR), with breadth under a square root.
Carhart adds a fourth factor, momentum (UMD), to the Fama-French market, SMB and HML factors.
The regression version is ex post: realised excess return R_i - R_F with an alpha intercept. The FF expected-return model is ex ante: E(r_i) = r_f + betas x expected factor premia, with no alpha.
The market-timing regression adds a bull-market dummy term M_P(R_M - R_F)D to the CAPM regression; a significant positive M_P indicates timing ability.
CAPM prices only one factor, market beta times the market risk premium; the multifactor model sums beta_k x E(f_k) over K factors.
The CAPM market premium is average risk aversion times market VARIANCE, gamma*sigma_m^2; active risk aversion is backed out as IR / (2 x active risk sigma_A).
The discount-rate model divides the payoff by (1+E(r_i)); the SDF model multiplies the payoff by m inside the expectation.
Price form: P = E[m x payoff]. Return form: 1 = E[m(1+r)], obtained by dividing through by price.
For a risky asset m stays inside the expectation with (1+r_i); for the risk-free asset 1+r_f is known, so 1/(1+r_f) = E(m).
The SDF premium is beta on m (cov with m / var m) times a negative price of risk, so assets that pay off in bad times earn less; CAPM beta is measured against the market return.

IR_p is just the portfolio's alpha over its active risk, mu_p/omega_p. The manager weight uses IR_p as an input: (IR_i x portfolio TE) / (IR_p x manager TE), which gives more risk to more skilled managers. Don't invert the TE ratio.
Sharpe divides excess return by total risk sigma (for undiversified portfolios); Treynor divides by systematic risk beta (for well-diversified portfolios).
M^2 rescales the Sharpe ratio to market volatility: R_F + Sharpe x sigma_M, then subtracts the market return, giving a percentage return difference rather than a ratio.
Jensen's alpha measures return above the CAPM (beta-based) required return; M^2 measures return above the market after matching total risk sigma.
IR uses return minus benchmark over the tracking error sigma_(A-B); Sharpe uses return minus risk-free over total sigma_A.
HPR is one-period (income + capital gain) / initial investment; time-weighted return compounds the (1+r_t) terms and takes the 1/n root minus 1.
Allocation = (w_P - w_B) x benchmark return R_B; selection = portfolio weight w_P x (R_P - R_B). Weight difference versus return difference.
Total contribution w_P R_P - w_B R_B is the sum of allocation and selection. Don't report the selection term alone as the total.
Active risk aversion lambda_A = IR/(2 sigma_A) is an input; MCVA = alpha_n - 2 lambda_A psi MCAR_n uses it again with a factor of 2 in the penalty term.
LCR = HQLA / 30-day net cash outflows (short-term survival); NSFR = available stable funding / required stable funding (one-year structural funding).
Dollar spread p = offer - bid; proportional spread s divides that by the MID price (not bid or offer).
Normal market uses the actual spread s_i; stressed market replaces it with mu_i + lambda*sigma_i. Both are halved and multiplied by position size alpha_i.
Both are VaR plus a liquidation cost. Normal adds sum of s*alpha/2; stressed adds sum of (mu + lambda*sigma)*alpha/2.
Exogenous-spread LVaR ADDS the half-spread cost to VaR; orderly-liquidation LVaR MULTIPLIES one-day VaR by sqrt[(1+T)(1+2T)/(6T)], which equals 1 at T = 1 and grows more slowly than sqrt(T).
Expected cost = P*s/2; the 99% confidence bound adds a 2.33*sigma_s spread cushion INSIDE the half: P*(s + 2.33*sigma_s)/2.

Both widen the spread by a multiple of its volatility. Malz's 99% interval fixes the multiple at 2.33 on the expected (mean) spread s for a single position P, written as a +/- range. Hull's stressed liquidation cost uses mu_i + lambda*sigma_i for a chosen lambda and sums over positions.
LTR LVaR scales one VaR by a T-day orderly-liquidation factor; the FRTB ES combines liquidity-horizon buckets as a square root of summed squares, scaled by sqrt((LH_j - LH_{j-1})/10).
cfaR+ = EXPECTED minus ACTUAL inflow (shortfall); cfaR- = ACTUAL minus EXPECTED outflow (excess). The order flips so both stay positive.
TSCF+ is built from inflow cfaR+ at quantile alpha; TSCF- is built from outflow cfaR- at 1 - alpha.
TSECF is the expected-cash-flow maturity ladder; TSLaR takes the adverse-quantile cash flow net of CUMULATIVE expected flows AND cumulative liquidity-generation capacity.
TSCLGC is only the running sum of liquidity-generation capacity; it is one of the two terms subtracted inside TSLaR, not the LaR itself.
Liquidity gap = change in deposits - change in loans (positive = surplus); AFG = desired loans/investments - expected funds (positive = must borrow). The sign conventions are opposite.
Net liquidity position nets ALL sources and uses of cash (including borrowings, expenses and dividends); the liquidity gap uses only estimated changes in deposits and loans.

The structure-of-funds requirement applies 95/30/15% reserve weights to hot, vulnerable and stable funds net of legal reserves; the expected requirement probability-weights scenario liquidity gaps G_i.
Hot money ratio = money-market ASSETS / volatile LIABILITIES (higher = more liquid, not a total-assets ratio); cash position = (cash + due from banks) / total assets.
Capacity ratio = net loans and leases / total assets (higher = LESS liquid); loan commitments ratio uses UNUSED commitments (contingent drawdowns) over total assets.
Core deposit ratio = core deposits / TOTAL ASSETS; deposit composition = demand deposits / TIME deposits.
Liquid securities indicator = US govt securities / TOTAL ASSETS (higher = more liquid); pledged securities ratio = pledged / total SECURITIES (higher = LESS liquid).
Weighted avg interest expense = interest only / total funds raised; break-even rate adds OTHER OPERATING COSTS and divides by EARNING assets only.
Overall cost of capital = break-even cost PLUS after-tax equity cost grossed up by 1/(1 - tax rate).
Same numerator (expected operating costs). Pooled funds expense divides by ALL new funds; the hurdle rate divides by dollars available for EARNING assets only, so it is higher.
Break-even rate is HISTORICAL cost over all earning assets; the hurdle rate is the FORWARD-LOOKING pooled-funds cost over dollars placeable in earning assets.
Ratio form F/S = (1+r)/(1+r*); premium form F - S = S[(1+r)/(1+r*) - 1]. Keep the domestic rate r in the numerator in both.
The post-2008 violation says the actual premium EXCEEDS the CIP-implied premium; the basis b is ADDED to the domestic rate r in the numerator to restore equality.
Dollar IS gap = ISA - ISL (positive = asset-sensitive); ISR = ISA / ISL (asset-sensitive when > 1, not > 0).
Relative IS gap divides the dollar gap by institution SIZE (total assets), not by ISL.
Change in NII = rate change x CUMULATIVE repricing gap (income view); change in NW uses durations and the discount factor on A and L (market-value view).
Leverage-adjusted gap scales liability duration by L/A: D_A - D_L*(L/A). The unadjusted gap omits that weight.
F07 is the accounting identity change in NW = change in A - change in L; F10 fills each term with -D x change in r/(1+r) x value, so a positive duration gap loses value when rates rise.
NIM = (interest income - interest expense) / earning assets, a spread earned; break-even cost rate = (interest + other operating costs) / earning assets, a cost to cover.
Value per 100 of CASH = 100 x days x special spread / 360; per 100 FACE multiplies that by price/100.
Yield value in bp divides the per-100-FACE value (not per-100-cash) by DV01.
Special spread = GC rate - special rate (positive for specials); that spread, not either rate alone, drives the financing value.
The stressed buffer is a DOLLAR waterfall (buffer - stressed outflows + stressed inflows); LCR is a RATIO of HQLA to 30-day NET outflows.

FTP = base rate + term liquidity premium + liquidity premium (the cushion's carry cost averaged over total assets); contingent liquidity cost prices the UNDRAWN share x likelihood of drawdown x cost of funding the cushion.
Plain RAROC is compared with the hurdle rate. Adjusted RAROC first subtracts beta_E x (R_M - R_F) and is then compared with the risk-free rate.

Both RAROCs net expected losses and tax out of the numerator. The difference is the denominator: credit RAROC divides loan revenues, loan value x (s + f - l - c)(1 - x), by capital at risk (the duration-based change in loan value, -L x D x di/(1+i)). Operational-risk RAROC divides after-tax risk-adjusted net income by economic capital.

The ORR numerator subtracts expected losses and taxes and ADDS the return on economic capital. The loan-revenue numerator is loan value x (spread + fees - loss - cost) x (1 - tax) and has no capital-return term.
The after-tax hurdle is the weighted average cost of common and preferred equity; Adjusted RAROC subtracts beta_E x (R_M - R_F) from RAROC and is then compared with R_F rather than the hurdle.
Same beta x (R_M - R_F) term with opposite sign. CAPM ADDS it to R_F to get the cost of equity. ARAROC SUBTRACTS it from RAROC.
Basel III total Tier 1 is at least 6% of RWA, of which CET1 is at least 4.5%. Basel I Tier 1 is only at least 4%.
Tier 1 (CET1 + AT1) is at least 6%. Total capital (Tier 1 + Tier 2) is at least 8%, or 10.5% with the conservation buffer.
The leverage ratio divides Tier 1 capital by total, un-risk-weighted exposure and needs at least 3%. The Tier 1 ratio divides by RWA and needs at least 6%.
LCR is HQLA over net cash outflows in a 30-day stress. NSFR is available stable funding over required stable funding over one year. Both must be at least 100%.
Under Basel I, Tier 1 must be more than 4% of RWA and total capital (Tier 1 + Tier 2) more than 8%.
The interest-rate add-on starts at 1% and adds 1% per year beyond the first. The FX add-on starts at 5% and adds 3% per year.
Capital = 0.08 x RWA, and RWA = 12.5 x capital. Do not multiply a VaR-based charge by 0.08, or RWA by 12.5.
Both use the multiplier m = 3 + k on average VaR. The ORR formula takes the max with yesterday's VaR and then multiplies by 12.5 to turn capital into market RWA.
Formula 1 sums EAD x LGD x DR99.9 and subtracts EL, with no maturity adjustment. Formula 2 is per exposure, uses (DR99.9 - PD) and multiplies by MA.
The IRB formula gives capital. RWA is the same product x 12.5.
The Basel II IRB charge uses (DR99.9 - PD) x MA, i.e. unexpected loss only. The credit-reading version multiplies by the full WCDR and subtracts neither PD nor applies MA.
Regulatory IRB capital is the 99.9% one-year VaR minus EL. The credit VaR example uses the 95th percentile minus EL. Watch the confidence level.
MA = [1 + (M - 2.5)b] / (1 - 1.5b) depends on maturity. b = [0.11852 - 0.05478 ln(PD)]^2 depends only on PD. Do not put M into b or ln(PD) into MA.
BI is the sum of the averaged income components (ILDC + SC + FC). BIC applies the marginal 12%/15%/18% coefficients to BI by bracket, not 18% to the whole of BI.
LC = 15 x the average annual loss over 10 years. ILM = ln[e - 1 + (LC/BIC)^0.8] and equals 1 when LC = BIC.
Capital for bucket 2 and 3 banks is BIC x ILM (bucket 1 uses BIC alone); the BIC itself is built from BI in marginal slices: 12% of the first EUR 1bn, 15% of the next 29bn, 18% above 30bn.
